Lecture 1 - Fei-Fei Li & Justin Johnson & Serena Yeung Our philosophy • Thorough and Detailed. – Understand how to write from scratch, debug and train convolutional neural networks. • Practical. – Focus on practical techniques for training these networks at scale, and on GPUs (e.g. will touch on distributed optimization, differences between CPU vs. GPU, etc.) Also look at state of the art software tools such as Caffe, TensorFlow, and (Py)Torch • State of the art. – Most materials are new from research world in the past 1-3 years. Lecture 1 - Fei-Fei Li & Justin Johnson & Serena Yeung Grading policy • 3 Problem Sets: 15% x 3 = 45% • Midterm Exam: 15% • Final Course Project: 40% – Milestone: 5% – Final write-up: 35% – Bonus points for exceptional poster presentation • Late policy – 7 free late days – use them in your ways – Afterwards, 25% off per day late – Not accepted after 3 late days per PS – Does not apply to Final Course Project • Collaboration policy – Read the student code book, understand what is ‘collaboration’ and what is ‘academic infraction’ 4/4/201744

levels.title: The History of Computer Vision
levels.goal: Trace the key breakthroughs and ideas that shaped computer vision over the decades.

units.mechanicReason: These discoveries happened in a specific historical sequence that must be reconstructed in order.

item.prompt: Put these milestones in computer vision in the order they happened.

steps.text: Hubel & Wiesel study how simple, complex, and hypercomplex cells respond to light orientation and movement.
Larry Roberts builds the 'Block World' program, extracting feature points from simple shapes.
Viola & Jones develop a practical face detection algorithm.

item.why: The dates attached to each milestone place neuroscience research first, early computer vision programs second, and automated face detection last.

hints: Think about which came first: studying how brain cells react to images, or building computer programs that analyze images.
One milestone is about cat brains, one is about simple block shapes, and one is about finding faces in real time.

variants.prompt: Arrange these computer vision discoveries chronologically.

steps.text: Researchers find that simple, complex, and hypercomplex cells respond differently to orientation and movement of light.
A program analyzes a 'Block World' scene, selecting feature points from an original picture.
An algorithm for detecting faces in images is introduced.

variants.why: Each discovery carries a year that fixes its place in the timeline, from brain cell studies to block-world vision to face detection.

points: Computer vision's history runs from 1950s brain-cell studies to early block-world programs to modern face detection and deep learning.
Marr's theory describes vision as moving through stages, from raw perceived intensities to a full 3-D model.
ImageNet organized millions of images into a large hierarchy of semantic categories, such as animals, plants, and artifacts.
CNNs became an important tool for object recognition only after decades of incremental research, not overnight.

points: CS231n centers on image classification as one of the key visual recognition problems, but related tasks like object detection, image captioning, and action classification are also part of the field.
The course frames visual intelligence as a goal that goes far beyond just object recognition.
Grades are split into 3 Problem Sets (45%), a Midterm Exam (15%), and a Final Course Project (40%).
The late policy gives 7 free late days usable on problem sets (not the final project); after that it's 25% off per day, and problem sets aren't accepted more than 3 days late.
